author: blu
body: The two outcomes are named functions rather than branches written inline, because the accepting one has to load the key into pinned memory before it wipes the plaintext, and that load is effectful: inline it needs an act-bind nested inside an if inside an act, which is the exact shape that has scoped an `in` to the wrong `let` before now. A single-line dispatch to two named functions cannot do that. Both branches zero every plaintext buffer on every path -- the refusing one zeroes the same three the accepting one does, which is the property worth reading them side by side to check.

author: blu
body: These three reach the pinned key through key-zero and key-status, so they carry [Identity] and say so. The row is not bookkeeping: Identity is a real capability with a manifest bit, and a program that can lock, unlock, or ask after the private key is exercising authority a program that merely prints does not have. Declaring it here is what makes that authority visible in the signature of everything above -- up to and including first-boot's own entry point, which is the one place a reader should be able to see it.

author: blu
body: It has never mattered, and that is not a reason to leave it: the only caller is idm-generate-keypair, whose seed is idm-hash-words-to-bytes of a sha256 -- eight words, exactly 32 bytes -- so the short path was never taken. A helper that pads on request must pad, or the first caller with a shorter source gets a key built from a truncated seed and no error.

author: blu
body: Nothing in this loop had to change for it, which is the point of doing the conversion at the boundary: the loop collects what the keyboard says and never interprets it. Only the terminator moved, from the ASCII carriage return to `key-enter`, because Enter is not a character and never was.

author: blu
body: (historical) `poll-key` had no shift latch, so a letter arrived as its UPPERCASE ASCII code whatever the typist did, and a passphrase was folded to uppercase before it was ever hashed. This is a property of the stored identity, not of this loop: teaching `poll-key` to decode shift changed what these bytes are, and every passphrase created before that day stopped unlocking its key. Fold here deliberately, or migrate, but do not let it change by accident.

author: blu
body: The passphrase-derived AES-256 key. It was written out at all four sites that need it -- both encrypts and both decrypts -- and it was wrong at all four, in the same way: each ran hkdf's result through idm-hash-words-to-bytes.

author: blu
body: Nothing could see it. The same wrong key encrypted and decrypted, so the ceremony round-tripped: a passphrase set at first boot unlocked correctly, and the only symptom was a number nobody read. That is why it is one function now -- a derivation written four times is a derivation that can be wrong four times -- and why idm-key-tests asserts its LENGTH rather than round-tripping it. A round trip agrees with itself.
